evidence.text: Purpose: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) can introduce electrocardiogram (ECG) criteria that lack patient-specific measurement support. This study evaluates the reliability of retrieved diagnostic criteria in AI-generated ECG reports. Methods: We analyzed 1,083 human-validated PTB-XL patient records using a library of 47 criteria cards, including 33 without numeric verification rules. Language models generated structured reports with and without retrieval. Criterion applicability was evaluated using Marquette 12SL measurements, with independent assessment using Uni-G and comparison against expert-validated diagnostic labels. Results: Keyword retrieval introduced untestable or measurement-disconfirmed criteria in 46.8% of GPT-4.1-mini reports. A deterministic verification rule withdrew 647 criterion applications, including 639 without numeric checks, while preserving 268 of 269 applications independently supported by Uni-G. Restricting retrieval to 14 testable criteria reduced the initial unsupported-criterion rate to 13.8%. Under matched instructions and an identical output schema, retrieval increased unsupported-criterion reports from 17.4% to 31.1%, while hypertrophy recall remained unchanged at 62.6%. Conclusion: These findings identify a fundamental limitation of retrieval-based clinical report generation: retrieved criteria do not necessarily provide valid patient-specific evidence. Measurement-based verification can reduce unsupported criterion applications, but diagnostic validity requires independent assessment.

evidence.text: RAG-TRACE establishes a measurement-centered approach to assessing evidence reliability in AI-generated ECG reports. The evaluation highlights the importance of distinguishing retrieved clinical information from criteria supported by patient-specific measurements. Its verification mechanism provides a transparent means of identifying unsupported applications while preserving valid quantitative evidence. Importantly, criterion-level reliability and diagnostic completeness represent separate dimensions of report quality that require independent assessment. Integrating these principles into clinical RAG pipelines could support more interpretable and auditable AI-generated reports. Future work should extend RAG-TRACE to broader clinical datasets, incorporate measurement-aware retrieval, and evaluate its impact through clinician-adjudicated assessments.

evidence.text: PTB-XL version 1.0.3 comprises 21,799 ECG recordings from 18,869 patients Wagner et al. (2020) . The diagnostic cohort includes 21,375 recordings from 18,610 patients, annotated across five superclasses: normal, myocardial infarction, ST/T change, conduction disturbance, and hypertrophy. Patient-disjoint folds 1–8, 9, and 10 were assigned to training, calibration, and testing, respectively. Sex was encoded as 0 for male and 1 for female. All calibration and test records contained human-validated diagnostic labels, which served as the reference standard without additional clinical adjudication. ECG measurements were obtained from PTB-XL+ version 1.0.1 Strodthoff et al. (2023) . Marquette 12SL provided the primary measurements for criterion verification, with Uni-G serving as an independent reference. The 12SL-based verification used Uni-G exclusively for subsequent assessment, while the agreement-based configuration required concordant support from both algorithms. ECGDeli was included in measurement agreement analyses. All measurements were derived from published feature tables, without additional signal delineation or model training. Diagnostic probabilities for the five superclasses were estimated using one-versus-rest histogram gradient-boosting classifiers trained with inverse-frequency weighting, a learning rate of 0.08, a maximum of 31 leaves, and 120 iterations with early stopping. Class-specific isotonic calibration was performed on fold 9 Niculescu-Mizil and Caruana (2005) , followed by evaluation on the held-out fold 10. Diagnostic assertions with calibrated probabilities below 0.5 were classified as low-probability, solely for analytical purposes.

evidence.text: The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) is an essential diagnostic tool for assessing cardiac activity through measurable intervals, axes, and voltages Kligfield et al. (2007) ; Mason et al. (2007) . Large datasets such as PTB-XL, comprising 21,799 recordings from 18,869 patients Wagner et al. (2020) , have advanced automated ECG interpretation Strodthoff et al. (2021) . Deep learning models have achieved strong performance in detecting cardiac abnormalities Ribeiro et al. (2020) ; Hannun et al. (2019) ; Alday et al. (2020) ; Mehari and Strodthoff (2022) and supporting cardiovascular screening Attia et al. (2019) ; Siontis et al. (2021) . Nevertheless, generating reliable clinical reports requires more than diagnostic predictions. Each reported finding must be supported by patient-specific evidence. Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential for generating clinical narratives Tu et al. (2025) and diagnostic explanations Singhal et al. (2023) ; Nori et al. (2023) . Their outputs can contain unsupported statements and inaccurate evidence attribution Ji et al. (2023) ; Maynez et al. (2020) . Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) incorporates external knowledge to improve factual grounding Lewis et al. (2020) ; Gao et al. (2024) ; Shuster et al. (2021) , with promising applications in medical question answering Xiong et al. (2024) ; Zakka et al. (2024) and clinical information extraction Agrawal et al. (2022) . Recent studies have investigated evidence alignment in clinical question answering Irankhah and Fodeh (2026) and query-level reliability in retriever upgrades Irankhah and Arif (2026) . These advances highlight the importance of evidence quality, but the reliability of retrieved criteria in ECG report generation remains insufficiently examined

evidence.text: For the eight criteria linked to cardiologist statement codes, keyword retrieval increased statement mismatch from 7.5% to 24.9% for GPT-4.1 mini and from 1.6% to 34.1% for Qwen3-8B. The two-algorithm agreement rule reduced these rates to 22.2% and 19.6%, respectively, without a substantial increase in unstated linked findings (Table 5 ). Among retained applications, the linked code was present in 27.5% of 204 GPT-4.1 mini applications and 12.8% of 218 Qwen3-8B applications. Numeric support and diagnostic-label agreement therefore remained distinct. Statement mismatch against stored cardiologist codes for the original eight checks, and the mean number of those findings left unstated.

evidence.text: Following 12SL withdrawal, Uni-G rejection decreased from 5.3% to 4.6% for GPT-4.1-mini and from 20.8% to 4.7% for Qwen3-8B. Of 647 GPT-4.1 mini withdrawals, 639 involved unchecked cards and eight involved failed numeric predicates. Uni-G independently rejected seven of those eight predicates. For Qwen3-8B, the corresponding counts were 880 unchecked applications and 211 failed predicates, of which Uni-G rejected 203. Verification retained 268 of 269 Uni-G-supported applications for GPT-4.1 mini and 274 of 282 for Qwen3-8B (Table 4 ). Uni-G was not an input to the 12SL withdrawal rule. Keyword-note applications judged by Uni-G. Uni-G was not an input to the 12SL edit. The second row is the subset of the failed 12SL predicates that Uni-G also rejected. The unchecked row is separate.
